schools.summary: Gill will not fix Joshua's age but reckons about a hundred, since he lived to a hundred and ten and the Jews commonly allow seven years for the dividing of Canaan, which he did not long survive. Calvin denies that old and stricken in years is a tautology, the Jews having used a threefold division of age whose last stage runs from the eightieth year to the end of life. He allows that a pause after thirty-one kings had fallen was reasonable, provided they rested only for a time, but holds that the Lord applies a new spur by ordering even the enemy-held coast into the lot; the procedure might look absurd and ludicrous, a complete mockery, yet the lot was to be an earnest of certain possession, and those whose portion fell in enemy country, living as strangers on precarious hospitality, would act as taskmasters spurring the rest on. It had to be done while Joshua lived, no successor having authority enough for so difficult a task.

Henry notes that Joshua and Caleb were by now the only old men in Israel, none of those numbered at Sinai being left alive but the two, and that Joshua, a man of war from his youth, was yielding to infirmities against which it is vain for the stoutest to contend; comparing him with Moses he observes that all who reach old age do not find it alike good. He makes the divine reminder itself the lesson, since some have grey hairs upon them and perceive it not and need telling, and draws two consequences: that Joshua should lay aside the pursuit of the war, being gathered to his rest with honour while the conquering of the skirts is left to those who came after, since God considers the frame of his people; and that what he could still do he must do quickly, all people and old people especially setting about what must be done before they die.

Clarke gives the same age and apportions the years, seven in the conquest, one in the division, ten before his death, and thinks Joshua had meant to subdue the whole land before dividing it, God not allowing it because Israel's unfaithfulness made it fit that some old inhabitants should remain to keep them in check and each tribe have labour of its own. Wesley keeps only the point that the aged should be reminded of their age.

Keil and Delitzsch set the command at the head of the whole distribution, entered upon now that Joshua was old although parts of the country were still unconquered, with the account of the eastern territory appended.

themes: Joshua was old and stricken in years
there remaineth yet very much land
why divide what is not yet possessed
the lot as an earnest of possession

schools.summary: Gill says the catalogue was given for Joshua's information, that he might know what he had to divide, and for the people's, that they might know their claim and what the Lord would deliver into their hands provided they were obedient; because they were not, many of these places never came into their possession though divided to them by lot. Calvin reads the list as a recalling of the ancient boundaries fixed by God, so that the people might be persuaded the covenant with Abraham would be fulfilled in every part, and turns it into a rule of perseverance, since Paul forgets what is behind and presses toward the mark. He raises the question nobody else asks, why a sixth people, the Avites, follows five counted sea-coast territories, and proposes an antithesis between a free people, their own masters, and five territories under sovereigns. On the promise itself he draws the positive lesson, that Joshua must not defer the partition for want of possession, since doubt of the event would detract from God's honour.

Clarke prints a friend's opinion against identifying Sihor with the Nile, names the five lordships as Gaza, Ashdod, Askalon, Gath and Ekron, marks Ekron the most northern and says there is no proof Israel ever held it, warns that the Avites are not the Hivites but a tribe already dispossessed by the Caphtorim, and reports Calmet's proposal to read Aramites for Amorites, an emendation of two letters that Houbigant approves though no version supports it. On the promise to drive out the hill country and the Sidonians he insists the word was never unconditional, and meets the charge that Scripture failed by distinguishing what was promised: Joshua was to bring them in and divide the land, which he did, not to conquer the whole first. Wesley states the condition flatly and keeps both halves of the promise, that God will do his work in his own time yet that driving out before the children of Israel supposes they must go up against them.

Keil and Delitzsch settle the southern boundary against the Nile, which is always called simply the river in plain prose and flowed through the middle of Egypt rather than before it, and identify the Sichor here with the brook of Egypt; they also distinguish the Geshuri of this verse from the Geshur of Peraea. On the northern names they identify the Giblites with Gebal, the Byblos of the Greeks, on the coast north of Beirut.

debates.question: Is the Sihor before Egypt the Nile?

sides.position: yes, with Jarchi and Kimchi, though perhaps a branch rather than the river itself
no; the Nile is always called simply the river and flows through Egypt, not before it — this is the brook of Egypt

themes: this is the land that yet remaineth
the five lords of the Philistines
is Sihor the Nile or the brook of Egypt?
them will I drive out from before you

7.pericope_label: The command to divide, and the eastern inheritance

schools.summary: Gill notes only that with God's authority for it Joshua was to begin at once, that Reuben and Gad had asked for their portion and so had no share in this division, that Aroer was a Moabite city on the Arnon, and that Israel expelled neither the Geshurites nor the Maachathites under Moses or Joshua. Calvin thinks the notice about Levi necessary, lest the Levites allege they were unjustly disinherited and raise commotions about their right; Moses is named as the author of the distinction, and an excellent compensation was given, for as God allures them by hire to the charge of sacred things, he binds the people to pay the oblations that maintain them.

Henry catches the exchange behind the command, Joshua thinking all must be conquered before any could be divided and God answering that enough is conquered to serve their turn, from which he takes it that we must have the comfort of what we have though we cannot compass all we would. He draws three things from the order: that the land must be divided at all, since it is the will of the God who gave the earth to men that every man should know his own and the world be governed by equity and not arms; that it must be an inheritance though won by conquest, since what is got by force is soon lost while a title by divine grant is secured to the seed; and that it must go by lot rather than by Joshua's will, the lot referring the matter wholly to God. In dividing what he conquered Joshua was a type of Christ, and the recital of the eastern grant explains why only nine tribes and a half are provided for, gives Joshua a pattern, and spurs him to hasten; the repeated words ratify the grant, so that as Moses settled it, so shall it rest.

Clarke states plainly that the two tribes and the other half of Manasseh had their portion in the land of Og and Sihon. Wesley turns the repeated words into an instruction that Joshua is not to disturb those possessions but to divide the rest, traces Medeba and Dibon from Moab to the Amorites to Israel and back again at the captivity, and observes that God had given the Geshurite and Maachathite land away though the gift went unused; he says the notice about Levi is repeated to guard them against the malice, envy and covetousness of their brethren.

Keil and Delitzsch take Gilead for the whole country of that name on both sides of the Jabbok and mark the awkwardness that the Geshurite and Maachathite territory is counted into the inheritance although it was never possessed and had probably never been subject to Og; they explain that Levi received no land but the firings of Jehovah, the offerings with tithes and firstfruits, so that God himself is called Levi's inheritance.

themes: divide this land for an inheritance
the lot rather than Joshua’s own will
the two tribes and a half already settled
only unto the tribe of Levi he gave none inheritance

schools.summary: Gill gives the short notes on the towns, explaining Beth-peor from Peor the Moabite idol, where a temple to it had likely stood, and passing on Kimchi's guess that Balaam went back to Midian for his wages once his counsel took effect, with the Jewish account that Phinehas killed him. Calvin asks why so much detail was needed and gives two reasons, gratitude, the divine goodness being recorded in public documents and kept before the people's eyes, and peace, since human cupidity is ingenious in devising pretexts for litigation and this country had been given without casting lots; the boundaries are therefore fixed by God's own authority, traced from Aroer round the whole circuit so as to leave not a single acre ambiguous, and the care God took to cherish peace shows a truly paternal love. On the princes he notes that they are called satraps to show they fell in the same overthrow, having joined an unjust war, and that Balaam is named among the slain because his tongue had tried to wound Israel worse than a thousand swords.

Clarke places Kirjathaim nine miles east of Medeba on Eusebius's authority and traces its owners from the Emim through the Moabites and Amorites to Israel, adding from Calmet that Moab took it back when Reuben went into captivity; on the mount of the valley he supposes a town on a hill in flat country. He takes the opposite view to Ellicott on the Balaam notice, holding that both verses seem borrowed from Numbers and that Balaam's death is quite irrelevant here. Wesley notes that the division by families holds of the greater families only, reads the mount of the valley as the mountain bordering a valley then famous in Israel and thinks the clause belongs to all the cities named, and says the notice about Balaam is repeated because the turning of that curse into a blessing deserved everlasting remembrance.

Keil and Delitzsch place Reuben's portion in the south, from Aroer in the Arnon valley across the table-land by Medeba with Heshbon its capital, note that Heshbon lay on the border and was ceded to Gad, who gave it to the Levites, that Dibon is called Dibon of Gad because the Gadites fortified it, that Bamoth-baal is to be sought on the Jebel Attarus, and that Sibmah has hopelessly disappeared. Ellicott seizes on the naming of the Midianite princes as dukes of Sihon, which supplies a reason for the war beyond the one Numbers gives, since the Midianites were part of Sihon's government; he calls this, and the epithet soothsayer given to Balaam, undesigned agreements between Joshua and the Pentateuch.

debates.question: Why is Balaam’s death recorded here?

sides.position: it is an undesigned agreement with the Pentateuch, and the epithet soothsayer supplies what Numbers only hints
the verses seem borrowed from Numbers, and the notice is quite irrelevant in this place

themes: the boundaries fixed to prevent disputes
the cities of the plain by Medeba
the princes of Midian, dukes of Sihon
Balaam the soothsayer slain with the sword

24.pericope_label: The inheritance of Gad and of half Manasseh

schools.summary: Gill notes that Jazer, Gad's southern limit, is spoken of as a city of Moab by the later prophets, identifies Ramath-mizpeh with Ramoth-gilead, which Jerome knew as a village two miles from Rabbath, confesses that Betonim is nowhere else mentioned, and leaves open whether the half tribe asked for its eastern portion or had it unprompted. Calvin ends on the two things the list is for: God is extolled for his liberality in expelling nations of great celebrity and putting Israel in their room, which the counting of sixty cities makes plain, so that nobody may think Moses munificent by mistake; and the exclusion of Levi is repeated in a short clause lest the Levites afterwards pretend that a grant made without casting lots belonged to them in common, since here it is not the sacrifices but God himself who is called their inheritance, and if they are not satisfied with that they convict themselves of insufferable pride.

Clarke states the principle that Israel might not take Ammonite land but held this portion by conquest, having taken it with Sihon's kingdom, adds that Ramath-mizpeh was a city of refuge, gives Mahanaim as the two camps north of the brook Jabbok where Jacob saw the two camps of angels, reports that Herod rebuilt Beth-aram and named it Livias after the wife of Augustus though Josephus calls it Julias, derives Succoth from Jacob's pitching his tents there, and raises the question why half of Manasseh was settled east of the river at all when no part of the tribe had joined Reuben and Gad's request, answering that it was numerous and had much cattle. Wesley agrees that the Ammonite land meant is what had anciently been theirs until the Amorites took it, notes that only cities of eminence are meant by the cities of Gilead, reads the boundary as excluding Mahanaim itself, and offers two further motives for the eastern settlement, a recompense to Machir for his acts against Og and the better defence of the other two tribes.

Keil and Delitzsch set out Gad's territory as Jazer and the towns of southern Gilead, the northern half having been Og's and going to Manasseh, with the boundary running north to the Jabbok and passing beyond it only at Mahanaim while in the Jordan valley it reached the Sea of Galilee; they take half the land of the children of Ammon for the strip between the Arnon and the Jabbok that Sihon's Amorites had taken from Ammon. Manasseh's territory they run from Mahanaim over all Bashan with the sixty towns of Jair and the northern half of Gilead, and they mark the last two verses as the closing formula and a repetition of the earlier notice on Levi.

themes: half the land of the children of Ammon
Mahanaim and the border of Gad
why half Manasseh settled east of Jordan
the Lord God of Israel was their inheritance
